items.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002
items.q: I went with Scobey for a year and got the Dixieland experience.

ctx.x: Well music is like so many forms of art, it’s a labor of love. And the music business, you talk about being addictive, it’s as addictive as any narcotic man. I mean once you start playing, especially if you’re playing with guys that can play and you get a certain cohesiveness and a certain satisfaction. And then the people, the audience, you bring so much joy to them. Husband and wife, or girlfriend and boyfriend, or fiancees, they’ll come out and maybe that’s a very memorable night to them. Maybe you played…

why I went to work for the union, in 1965. So I got a job with the union and so at least I could pay my rent and everything. So then I could afford to be a casual musician. So I would get casual work on the weekends, then I got most of my jobs, I was lucky, they were long term jobs. With Vernon Alley — I worked with Vernon Alley. He was the house band leader for the Black Hawk. And I worked with Vernon because we had been in the Navy together. I worked with him I guess maybe three or four years. Then when they…
That’s interesting because he’s the first fella you recorded with, isn’t he?
